summary: Reports on the IAB workshop on Stack Evolution in a Middlebox Internet, held in Zurich in January 2015. It looked at how to evolve the transport layer when middleboxes and interfaces make the stack hard to change, and aimed to produce guidance for future work.

eli5.summary: A group of experts met to figure out how to improve the Internet's plumbing when boxes in the middle block new designs.

questions: why is it hard to evolve transport protocols
why do middleboxes block new protocols
how can new transport protocols be deployed
subtitle: How middleboxes block new transport protocols and what to do about it

tldr.problem: The Internet's transport layer has become ossified: middleboxes inspect and modify packets, and hardware devices have been deployed that make assumptions about existing protocols. This prevents innovation in how programs communicate.
tldr.mechanism: An IAB workshop in Zurich brought together experts to discuss the problem and identify approaches to evolve transport in the presence of middlebox constraints, including encryption, UDP encapsulation, and cooperative signaling.
tldr.outcome: The workshop identified several work items: SPUD (Substrate Protocol for User Datagrams) for signaling, middlebox measurement efforts, updated guidelines for middlebox deployment, and architectural guidance for transport evolution.

today: The SEMI workshop report catalyzed subsequent work on transport protocol evolution, middlebox measurement, and encryption-based approaches to ossification. SPUD did not become a working group but influenced later work on transport extensibility and path-aware networking.

sections.title: A Stalled Internet
sections.content:
The Internet's transport layer—the rules that programs use to send data reliably—has become frozen in place. Middleboxes (firewalls, NATs, proxies, and other devices in the network) inspect packets and make assumptions about protocols like TCP and UDP. They block or modify packets that do not match their expectations. Application programmers who want to use new transport protocols cannot deploy them because middleboxes will break them. At the same time, existing protocols like TCP were designed decades ago and do not meet the needs of modern applications like WebRTC, which require low latency and flexible reliability settings.

Previous efforts (MIDCOM, NSIS, BEHAVE in the IETF) have tackled middlebox problems, but a new opportunity exists: encryption is now ubiquitous, making many packet inspection and modification operations obsolete. This creates a chance to improve how the Internet can evolve.
sections.eli5: Middleboxes are like border guards that only recognize old types of packages. New types of communication cannot get through. This meeting asked: how do we convince the guards to let new packages through?

sections.title: Why Ossification Happened and How to Fix It
sections.content:
Middlebox ossification exists because of economic incentives. Network operators deploy middleboxes to add value and manage their networks. Equipment vendors profit from selling more functionality. Moore's Law made it cheap to add processing power on-path. Enterprises find it more cost-effective to deploy functionality in the network than on endpoints. All these forces reinforce ossification.

The workshop identified that encryption is a powerful lever. When a transport protocol runs inside encryption (like UDP over DTLS), middleboxes cannot inspect or modify it. This resets the transport-versus-middlebox contest by making inspection impossible above the encryption layer. Any new protocol using this approach must offer better performance or functionality (like lower setup latency) than existing approaches to drive deployment.

Success requires aligning incentives for all parties: network operators, application developers, equipment vendors, and enterprises. Protocols that work anywhere, use the most efficient mechanism available, and remain simple to implement tend to win deployment.
sections.eli5: Middleboxes exist because it makes money for vendors and gives operators control. Encryption breaks middlebox inspection. New protocols need to be better and easier to deploy than old ones.

sections.title: Middleboxes: The Problem and Potential Solutions
sections.content:
The workshop noted that middleboxes cause unpredictability: operators cannot predict what will work on a given network path. A "bestiary" of middleboxes—a classification of impairments they cause—would help protocol designers know which workarounds matter. Middleboxes add queues and increase latency (bufferbloat), harming latency-sensitive applications. Network Function Virtualization (NFV) allows faster updates to middleboxes, but service chaining may add more middleboxes, increasing complexity.

Two competing visions emerged during the workshop: the "TCP Liberation Front" proposes fixing TCP and its extensions for broader deployment, while the "People's Front of UDP" proposes encapsulating new protocols inside UDP to bypass middlebox inspection. UDP encapsulation works but must be adapted for each use case—a long and painful process. TCP extensions have their own deployment problems. The workshop concluded both approaches have merit and different use cases.

Bob Briscoe's "Inner Space" proposal extends TCP headers within the TCP payload, where middleboxes cannot inspect them, offering a middle ground.
sections.eli5: Some middleboxes block new ideas. We could fix TCP, or we could hide new protocols inside UDP. Both work, but both have trade-offs.

sections.title: Work Items: SPUD, Measurement, and Guidance
sections.content:
The workshop identified four major work items. SPUD (Substrate Protocol for User Datagrams) would provide minimal signaling atop UDP—at least indication of first and last packets in a flow to help firewalls and NATs—plus optional application-to-path and path-to-application signaling. It would cooperate with encrypted transport (DTLS) to selectively expose information about encrypted flows. A BoF at IETF 92 produced prototype specifications, but discussion revealed requirements: any selective exposure must be declarative (not negotiated), advisory (not imperative), and independently verifiable. Basic transport must work even if signaling is ignored.

Middlebox Measurement work aims to gather data on how prevalent certain impairments are. Error logs from TCP stacks and applications on clients and servers can reveal when attempts to use particular transport features failed, providing opportunities to measure the network as a side effect of normal use.

The workshop also identified needs for updated guidelines on middlebox design and deployment and architectural guidance for transport stack evolution, including tradeoffs between user-space and kernel implementations, UDP encapsulation considerations, and cooperation between endpoints and the network.
sections.eli5: The workshop produced a to-do list: make a shim protocol (SPUD) for signaling, measure how many middleboxes block things, update deployment guidelines, and write architecture guides.

sections.title: The Role of Ossification and Cooperation
sections.content:
The workshop emphasized that not all paths are ossified. Michael Welzl pointed out that many network paths do not have problematic middleboxes, so endpoints could probe paths or use a happy-eyeballs-like approach to detect working protocols and fall back gracefully. This requires the TAPS (Transport Services) working group to decouple applications from specific transport protocols.

The workshop also stressed that the end-to-end argument—a fundamental principle in Internet design—has been compromised by middleboxes. Recovering some balance requires matching paths through the Internet with certain characteristics to application requirements. Rather than assuming all paths are identical, endpoints must discover path characteristics and adapt their approach.

Cooperation between endpoints and middleboxes could help, but enforcement of contracts between them requires extensive tunneling in less cooperative environments (illustrated by Costin Raiciu's "ninja tunneling" proposal).
sections.eli5: Not all networks have bad middleboxes, so programs could try different approaches and use the one that works. The trick is not relying on any single approach.
